prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory

statement.case_for: I moved my preferred prize from B023 (my opening first place) to B018 after reading colleagues' attribution arguments. IceCube is a discovery in the sense I care about: nature supplied a clue we did not predict, namely a diffuse flux of TeV-PeV neutrinos that is far above atmospheric expectations and independently confirmed in several analyses and detection channels, opening a new messenger channel for astronomy. It required a genuinely new instrument, a cubic-kilometre Cherenkov array in Antarctic ice, and it complements the 2002 prize for cosmic neutrinos without duplicating it. The credited pair, Halzen as conceiver and leader and Karle as central figure in construction and operation, is compact and fits the prize rules far better than my own B023 or the Higgs ballot B035, where any three names leave out decisive people. The Pearce and my own opening rankings both put this first or near it, and the prize is also easy to state in a single sentence.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a large collaboration of several hundred people stands behind the result, and two names inevitably simplify who did what; the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers are not recognised, and I have not verified from the supplied evidence which analysis or person was decisive for the first events. Maturity is also a fair concern: the identity of the dominant sources is unsettled, source associations such as TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane are statistically limited, and only IceCube holds the cleanest data set, so independent confirmation by KM3NeT and Baikal is still developing. If the committee decided that a prize should wait for source astronomy rather than diffuse-flux discovery, B040, which is already confirmed across many independent laboratories, would be the safer choice.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B040 first as a concrete, coherent, mature achievement, and ranks B018 fifth as plausibly a few years early because source-level astronomy is still developing.
responses.response: I take the clock case seriously, and I did not rank B040 in my opening, which I now regard as a gap in my own assessment. But I would separate the discovery from the programme: the prize for B018 would be for the diffuse astrophysical flux, which several analyses have confirmed, not for resolving the sources, just as 2002 honoured detection rather than a completed neutrino astronomy. My hesitation about B040 is that it is chiefly an invention whose consequences, the redefinition of the second and relativistic geodesy, are still partly prospective, and its distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 precision prizes needs more argument than you suggest. I would not object strongly to B040, and I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Kroll weights advances in what can be measured and how accurately very heavily, and judges B040 distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize because lattice clocks reached the 1e-18 level.
responses.response: I agree that the accuracy gain is real and that Katori's magic-wavelength insight is original. Where I differ is that the 2005 prize (Hall and Hänsch, in the comb lineage that Ye's own earlier work belongs to) and the 2012 prize already honoured the two technical pillars, optical frequency combs and control of single quantum systems, so the committee would be rewarding a third step in one measurement lineage. B018 opens a new observational channel rather than refining one, which to me weighs more heavily. I also notice that you give B018 no place in your ranking, so I would like to hear whether that reflects doubt about its attribution or about its maturity.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B055) first for its architectural impact on superconducting processors, but flags the 2025 prize for superconducting-circuit quantum effects as overlapping.
responses.response: Your own reservation seems decisive to me. A prize in 2026 for circuit QED would follow the 2025 award for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits too closely, and the committee would need an unusually clear argument that cQED is a distinct discovery rather than the same platform story. I also note your conflict flag with Chalmers and WACQT, which is appropriate, and I would suggest that on B055 you be cautious about advocating at the allocation stage. I do not think the overlap is fatal, but I do not think B055 should displace a clean discovery with no recent prize in its own area.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the KPZ ballot B005 first as a deep stochastic-process result with experimental confirmation, and includes B035 (Higgs) at eighth, noting that any three-person allocation among the four credited leaders is hard to defend.
responses.response: I agree with your attribution judgement on B035, and it is why I no longer put the Higgs observation in my preferred prize despite its obvious importance; my own opening choice of two founders and one leader was, as I said, not uniquely fair. On B005 I recognise the conceptual elegance of the KPZ universality class, but the supplied credit omits the exact-solution contributors, and only one of the three names carries the decisive experiment; I am less sure than you that the committee could argue that this is more than a good result in a narrower area. I would regard it as a respectable but not leading candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a discovery of a new observational channel (B018) over an enabling invention with the broadest first-place support (B040).
Whether two names fairly represent IceCube given AMANDA and the wider collaboration, and whether the first-event analysis leaders ought to be considered.

Whether source-level evidence, in particular the TXS 0506+056 association and the Galactic plane, will be considered mature enough to back the citation, or whether the citation should be restricted to the diffuse flux.
Whether the B023 attribution problem (Bennett, Spergel, Page, with Puget and Sunyaev excluded) can be resolved at all; I am no longer confident that it can.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the shortlisted ballots. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) are not credited names on any shortlisted candidate. I work in theoretical cosmology and gravity, which is adjacent to B023 and B038, but I have no personal or institutional tie to those candidates.
